{{Short description|Trigonometric values in terms of square roots and fractions}}
{{Trigonometry}}

In mathematics, the values of the [[trigonometric functions]] can be expressed approximately, as in <math>\cos (\pi/4) \approx 0.707</math>, or exactly, as in <math>\cos (\pi/ 4)= \sqrt 2 /2</math>. While [[trigonometric tables]] contain many approximate values, the exact values for certain angles can be expressed by a combination of arithmetic operations and [[square root]]s. The angles with trigonometric values that are expressible in this way are exactly those that can be constructed with a [[straightedge and compass construction|compass and straight edge]], and the values are called [[constructible numbers]].

== Common angles ==

The trigonometric functions of angles that are multiples of 15°, 18°, or 22.5° have simple algebraic values. These values are listed in the following table for angles from 0° to 45°<ref name="Abramowitz 1972 loc=p. 74, 4.3.46">{{harvnb|Abramowitz|Stegun|1972|loc=p. 74, 4.3.46}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF), §4.17 Special Values and Limits|url=http://dlmf.nist.gov/4.17}}</ref> (see [[Exact_trigonometric_values#Constructible_values|below]] for proofs). In the table below, the label "Undefined" represents a ratio <math>1:0.</math> If the codomain of the trigonometric functions is taken to be the [[real numbers]] these entries are [[undefined (mathematics)|undefined]], whereas if the codomain is taken to be the [[projectively extended real numbers]], these entries take the value <math>\infty</math> (see [[division by zero]]).

For angles outside of this range, trigonometric values can be found by applying [[List of trigonometric identities#Reflections, shifts, and periodicity|reflection and shift identities]], such as

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{3}
&&\sin(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta)  &{}= \cos(\theta), \\[5mu]
&&\sin(2\pi + \theta)  &{}= \sin(\pi - \theta) &&{}=  \sin(\theta), \quad
&&\sin(\pi + \theta)  &&{}= \sin(-\theta)      &&{}= -\sin(\theta), \\[5mu]
&&\cos(2\pi + \theta)  &{}= \cos(-\theta)      &&{}=  \cos(\theta), \quad
&&\cos(\pi + \theta)  &&{}= \cos(\pi - \theta) &&{}= -\cos(\theta).
\end{alignat}</math>

For example, for any {{mvar|&theta;}} greater than {{sfrac|&pi;|4}}, to find its sine, follow these steps to instead operate within the range of 0 to {{sfrac|&pi;|4}}:
# While it is greater than 2&pi;, subtract 2&pi; from it. Now try to find {{math|sin({{mvar|&theta;}})}}.
# If it is greater than &pi;, subtract &pi; from it and try to find {{math|&minus;sin({{mvar|&theta;}})}}.
# If it is greater than {{sfrac|&pi;|2}}, subtract {{sfrac|&pi;|2}} from it and try to find {{math|cos({{mvar|&theta;}})}}.
# If it is greater than {{sfrac|&pi;|4}}, subtract it from {{sfrac|&pi;|2}}. If you are trying to find cosine due to step 3, now try to find {{math|sin({{mvar|&theta;}})}}. If you are trying to find sine because you did not enter step 3, try to find {{math|cos({{mvar|&theta;}})}}.

== Trigonometric numbers ==
A '''trigonometric number''' is a number that can be expressed as the [[sine and cosine|sine or cosine]] of a [[Rational number|rational]] multiple of {{pi}} [[radian]]s.<ref name="Niven">Niven, Ivan. ''Numbers: Rational and Irrational'', 1961. Random House. [[New Mathematical Library]], Vol. 1. {{ISSN|0548-5932}}. Ch. 5</ref> Since <math>\sin(x)=\cos(x-\pi/2),</math> the case of a sine can be omitted from this definition. Therefore any trigonometric number can be written as <math>\cos(2\pi k/n)</math>, where ''k'' and ''n'' are integers. This number can be thought of as the real part of the [[complex number]] <math>\cos(2\pi k/n) + i \sin(2\pi k/n)</math>. [[De Moivre's formula]] shows that numbers of this form are [[roots of unity]]:
:<math>\left(\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right) + i \sin\left(\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right)\right)^n = \cos(2\pi k) + i \sin(2\pi k) = 1.</math>

(Conversely, the real part of any root of unity is a trigonometric number.) Since the root of unity is a [[polynomial root|root]] of the polynomial ''x''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1, it is [[algebraic number|algebraic]]. Since the trigonometric number is the average of the root of unity and its [[complex conjugate]], and algebraic numbers are closed under arithmetic operations, every trigonometric number is algebraic.<ref name="Niven"/> The minimal polynomials of trigonometric numbers can be [[minimal polynomial of 2cos(2pi/n)|explicitly enumerated]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lehmer |first1=D. H. |title=A Note on Trigonometric Algebraic Numbers |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=1933 |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=165–166 |doi=10.2307/2301023|jstor=2301023 }}</ref> In contrast, by the [[Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem]], the sine or cosine of any non-zero algebraic number is always [[Transcendental number|transcendental]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Burger |first1=Edward B. |last2=Tubbs |first2=Robert |title=Making Transcendence Transparent: An intuitive approach to classical transcendental number theory |date=17 April 2013 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4757-4114-8 |page=44 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s63TBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA44 |language=en}}</ref>

By [[Niven's theorem]], the only rational trigonometric numbers are 0, 1, −1, 1/2, and −1/2.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Schaumberger |first=Norman |year=1974 |title=A Classroom Theorem on Trigonometric Irrationalities |journal=[[Two-Year College Mathematics Journal]] |jstor=3026991 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=73–76|doi=10.2307/3026991 }}</ref>

== Constructibility ==
An angle can be constructed with a compass and straightedge if and only if its sine (or equivalently cosine) can be expressed by a combination of arithmetic operations and square roots applied to integers.<ref name=Martin>{{citation|last=Martin|first=George E.|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-0629-3|isbn=0-387-98276-0|mr=1483895|publisher=Springer-Verlag, New York|series=Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics|title=Geometric Constructions|title-link=Geometric Constructions|year=1998}}</ref>{{page needed|date=September 2025}} Additionally, an angle that is a rational multiple of <math>\pi</math> radians is constructible if and only if, when it is expressed as <math>a\pi/b</math> radians, where ''a'' and ''b'' are [[relatively prime]] integers, the [[prime factorization]] of the denominator, ''b'', is the product of some [[power of two]] and any number of distinct [[Fermat prime]]s (a Fermat prime is a prime number one greater than a power of two).<ref name=Martin/>{{rp|46}}

Thus, for example, <math>2\pi/15 = 24^\circ</math> is a constructible angle because 15 is the product of the Fermat primes 3 and 5. Similarly <math>\pi/12 = 15^\circ</math> is a constructible angle because 12 is a power of two (4) times a Fermat prime (3). But <math>\pi/9 = 20^\circ</math> is not a constructible angle, since <math>9 = 3 \cdot 3</math> is not the product of ''distinct'' Fermat primes as it contains 3 as a factor twice, and neither is <math>\pi/7 \approx 25.714^\circ</math>, since 7 is not a Fermat prime.<ref name=Fraleigh>{{citation|first=John B.|last=Fraleigh|title=A First Course in Abstract Algebra|edition=5th|year=1994|publisher=Addison Wesley|isbn=978-0-201-53467-2|mr=0225619}}</ref>

It results from the above characterisation that an angle of an integer number of degrees is constructible if and only if this number of degrees is a multiple of {{math|3}}.

== Constructible values ==

=== 45° ===

From a [[List of trigonometric identities#Reflections|reflection identity]], <math>\cos(45^\circ) = \sin(90^\circ-45^\circ)=\sin(45^\circ)</math>. Substituting into the [[Pythagorean trigonometric identity]] <math>\sin(45^\circ)^2 + \cos(45^\circ)^2=1</math>, one obtains the [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] <math>2 \sin(45^\circ)^2 - 1 = 0</math>. Taking the positive root, one finds <math>\sin(45^\circ) = \cos(45^\circ) = 1/\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}/2</math>.

A geometric way of deriving the sine or cosine of 45° is by considering an isosceles right triangle with leg length 1. Since two of the angles in an isosceles triangle are equal, if the remaining angle is 90° for a right triangle, then the two equal angles are each 45°. Then by the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the hypotenuse of such a triangle is <math>\sqrt{2}</math>. Scaling the triangle so that its hypotenuse has a length of 1 divides the lengths by <math>\sqrt{2}</math>, giving the same value for the sine or cosine of 45° given above.

=== 30° and 60° ===

The values of sine and cosine of 30 and 60 degrees are derived by analysis of the [[equilateral triangle]]. In an equilateral triangle, the 3 angles are equal and sum to 180°, therefore each corner angle is 60°. Bisecting one corner, the [[special right triangle]] with angles 30-60-90 is obtained. By symmetry, the bisected side is half of the side of the equilateral triangle, so one concludes <math>\sin(30^\circ)=1/2</math>. The Pythagorean and reflection identities then give <math>\sin(60^\circ)=\cos(30^\circ)=\sqrt{1-(1/2)^2}=\sqrt{3}/2</math>.

=== 18°, 36°, 54°, and 72° ===

The value of <math>\sin(18^\circ)</math> may be derived using the [[List of trigonometric identities#Multiple-angle formulae|multiple angle formulas]] for sine and cosine.<ref>{{cite web|title=Exact Value of sin 18°|url=https://www.math-only-math.com/exact-value-of-sin-18-degree.html|website=math-only-math}}</ref> By the double angle formula for sine:
<math display=block>\sin(36^\circ) = 2\sin(18^\circ)\cos(18^\circ)</math>
By the triple angle formula for cosine:
<math display=block>\cos(54^\circ) = \cos^3(18^\circ) - 3\sin^2(18^\circ)\cos(18^\circ) = \cos(18^\circ)(1 - 4\sin^2(18^\circ))</math>
Since sin(36°) = cos(54°), we equate these two expressions and cancel a factor of cos(18°):
<math display=block>2\sin(18^\circ) = 1 - 4\sin^2(18^\circ)</math>
This quadratic equation has only one positive root:
<math display=block>\sin(18^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}</math>

The Pythagorean identity then gives <math>\cos(18^\circ)</math>, and the double and triple angle formulas give sine and cosine of 36°, 54°, and 72°. Then <math>\cos(36^\circ)=(\sqrt{5}+1)/4=\varphi/2</math>, where {{tmath|\varphi}} is the [[golden ratio]].

A geometric method of finding the sines of these angles comes from analyzing a regular pentagon. Two of its diagonals form an angle of 36° that can be inscribed in a circle, and one side of the pentagon forms a chord of the circle that subtends this inscribed angle. To compute the chord's length, form a quadrilateral from four points of the pentagon. If the diagonals each have a length of one, then applying [[Ptolemy's theorem]] to this quadrilateral gives the equation <math>x^2 + x - 1 = 0</math>, where ''x'' is the chord length. The positive root of this equation is this value:

<math display=block>\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}</math>

Bisecting the 36° angle then creates a right triangle with angles of 18° and 72°, and cuts the chord in half, giving the same value for the sine of 18° given above. The sine value of 72° then follows from the Pythagorean theorem, and the sine values for 36° and 54° follow from sin(18°) and the double- and triple-angle formulas.

=== Remaining multiples of 3° ===
:{{commons file|Exact_trigonometric_table_for_multiples_of_3°.jpg|a table of these exact values|p= }}

The sines and cosines of all other angles between 0 and 90° that are multiples of 3° can be derived from the angles described above and the [[List of trigonometric identities#Angle sum and difference identities|sum and difference formulas]]. Specifically,<ref name="Weiß">{{cite book |last1=Weiß |first1=Adam |title=Handbuch Der Trigonometrie |date=1851 |publisher=J. L. Schmid |pages=72–74 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L3QoAAAAcAAJ&dq=%22sin%2039%22%20%22sin%2042%22&pg=PA72 |language=de}}</ref>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
3^\circ &= 18^\circ-15^\circ, &
24^\circ &= 60^\circ - 36^\circ, &
51^\circ &= 36^\circ + 15^\circ, &
78^\circ &= 60^\circ + 18^\circ, &
\\
6^\circ &= 36^\circ - 30^\circ, &
27^\circ &= 45^\circ - 18^\circ, &
57^\circ &= 75^\circ - 18^\circ, &
81^\circ &= 45^\circ + 36^\circ, &
\\
9^\circ &= 45^\circ - 36^\circ, &
33^\circ &= 18^\circ + 15^\circ, &
63^\circ &= 45^\circ + 18^\circ, &
84^\circ &= 54^\circ + 30^\circ, &
\\
12^\circ &= 30^\circ - 18^\circ, &
39^\circ &= 54^\circ - 15^\circ, &
66^\circ &= 36^\circ + 30^\circ, &
87^\circ &= 72^\circ + 15^\circ. &
\\
15^\circ &= 45^\circ - 30^\circ, &
42^\circ &= 60^\circ - 18^\circ, &
69^\circ &= 54^\circ + 15^\circ, &
\\
21^\circ &= 36^\circ - 15^\circ, &
48^\circ &= 30^\circ + 18^\circ, &
75^\circ &= 45^\circ + 30^\circ, &

\end{align}</math>

For example, since <math>24^\circ = 60^\circ - 36^\circ</math>, its cosine can be derived by the cosine difference formula:
<math display=block>\begin{align}\cos(24^\circ) &= \cos(60^\circ)\cos(36^\circ) + \sin(60^\circ)\sin(36^\circ) \\[4mu]
&= \frac{1}{2}\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\frac{\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}}}{4}\\[6mu]
&= \frac{1 + \sqrt{5} + \sqrt{30-6\sqrt{5}}}{8}\end{align}</math>

=== Half angles ===

If the denominator, ''b'', is multiplied by additional factors of 2, the sine and cosine can be derived with the [[List of trigonometric identities#Half-angle formulae|half-angle formulas]]. For example, 22.5° ({{pi}}/8 rad) is half of 45°, so its sine and cosine are:<ref>{{cite journal |title=A Geometric Method of Finding the Trigonometric Ratios of 22&hairsp;½° and 75° |last=Durbha |first=Subramanyam |journal=Mathematics in School |volume=41 |number=3 |year=2012 |pages=22–23 |jstor=23269221}}</ref>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
\sin(22.5^\circ) &= \sqrt{\frac12\bigl(1 - \cos(45^\circ)\bigr)}
= \sqrt{\frac12\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)}
= \frac12\sqrt{2-\sqrt2} \\
\cos(22.5^\circ) &= \sqrt{\frac12\bigl(1 + \cos(45^\circ)\bigr)}
= \sqrt{\frac12\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)}
= \frac12\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}
\end{align}</math>

Repeated application of the half-angle formulas leads to [[nested radical]]s, specifically nested [[square root of 2|square roots of 2]] of the form <math>\sqrt{2 \pm \cdots}</math>. In general, the sine and cosine of most angles of the form <math>\beta / 2^n</math> can be expressed using nested square roots of 2 in terms of <math>\beta</math>. Specifically, if one can write an angle as
<!-- the indices are reversed with b_k in the paper being b_1 here, because IMO it makes more sense to number from left to right -->
<math display=block>\alpha = \pi \left(\frac{1}{2}-\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\prod_{j=1}^i b_j}{2^{i+1}}\right) = \pi \left (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{b_1}{4} - \frac{b_1 b_2}{8} - \frac{b_1 b_2 b_3}{16} - \ldots - \frac{b_1 b_2 \ldots b_k}{2^{k+1}}\right)</math>
where <math>b_k \in [-2,2]</math>{{Clarify|post-text=&mdash; what are the actual limits on b<sub>k</sub>?|reason=bk very obviously can be values other than -2 and 2, but if it's supposed to be in that range, does it need to be an integer? A rational?  Any real?|date=January 2026}} and <math>b_i</math> is -1, 0, or 1 for <math>i<k</math>, then<ref name="Servi2003">{{cite journal |last1=Servi |first1=L. D. |title=Nested Square Roots of 2 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=April 2003 |volume=110 |issue=4 |pages=326–330 |doi=10.1080/00029890.2003.11919968}}</ref>
<math display=block>
\cos(\alpha) = \frac{b_1}{2}\sqrt{2+b_2 \sqrt{2+b_3 \sqrt{2+\ldots+b_{k-1} \sqrt{2+2 \sin\left(\frac{\pi b_k}{4}\right)}}}}
</math>
and if <math>b_1 \neq 0</math> then<ref name="Servi2003"/>
<math display=block>
\sin(\alpha) = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 - b_2 \sqrt{2+b_3 \sqrt{2+b_4 \sqrt{2+\ldots+b_{k-1} \sqrt{2+2 \sin\left(\frac{\pi b_k}{4}\right)}}}}}
</math>
For example, <math>\frac{13 \pi}{32} = \pi\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{32}\right)</math>, so one has <math>(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)=(1,-1,1,-1)</math> and obtains:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\cos\left(\frac{13 \pi}{32}\right) &= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2+2 \sin\left(\frac{-\pi}{4}\right)}}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2}}}}\\
\sin\left(\frac{13 \pi}{32}\right) &= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2-\sqrt 2}}}
\end{align}</math>

=== Denominator of 17 ===
{{main|Heptadecagon}}

Since 17 is a Fermat prime, a regular [[heptadecagon|17-gon]] is constructible, which means that the sines and cosines of angles such as <math>2\pi/17</math> radians can be expressed in terms of square roots. In particular, in 1796, [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] showed that:<ref name="Jones">Arthur Jones, Sidney A. Morris, Kenneth R. Pearson, ''Abstract Algebra and Famous Impossibilities'', Springer, 1991, {{ISBN|0387976612}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=6dSIBBW87b8C&pg=PA178 p. 178.]</ref><ref name=Callagy>Callagy, James J. "The central angle of the regular 17-gon", ''Mathematical Gazette'' 67, December 1983, 290–292.</ref>
<math display=block>\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{17}\right) = \frac{-1+\sqrt{17}+\sqrt{34-2\sqrt{17}} + 2\sqrt{17+3\sqrt{17} - \sqrt{170+38\sqrt{17}}}}{16}</math>

The sines and cosines of related constructible angles measuring <math>\textstyle k \pi / (17\cdot 2^n)</math> radians (for integers {{tmath|k}} and {{tmath|n}}) can be derived from this one.

== Non-constructibility of 1° ==

As discussed in {{section link|#Constructibility}}, only certain angles that are rational multiples of <math>\pi</math> radians have trigonometric values that can be expressed with square roots. The angle 1°, being <math>\pi/180 = \pi/(2^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5)</math> radians, has a repeated factor of 3 in the denominator and therefore <math>\sin(1^\circ)</math> cannot be expressed using only square roots. A related question is whether it can be expressed using cube roots. The following two approaches can be used, but both result in an expression that involves the [[exponentiation#nth_roots_of_a_complex_number|cube root of a complex number]]. [[Galois theory]] shows that the [[casus irreducibilis]] cannot be expressed in terms of solely real radicals.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Villanueva |first1=Jay |title=On the ''casus Irreducibilis'' of solving the cubic equation |url=https://www.math.odu.edu/~bogacki/epictcm/VOL24/C036/paper.pdf}}</ref>

Using the triple-angle identity, we can identify <math>\sin(1^\circ)</math> as a root of a cubic polynomial: <math>\sin(3^\circ) = -4x^3 + 3x</math>. The three roots of this polynomial are <math>\sin(1^\circ)</math>, <math>\sin(59^\circ)</math>, and <math>-\sin(61^\circ)</math>. Since <math>\sin(3^\circ)</math> is constructible, an expression for it could be plugged into [[Cubic_equation#Cardano's_formula|Cardano's formula]] to yield an expression for <math>\sin(1^\circ)</math>. However, since all three roots of the cubic are real, this is an instance of casus irreducibilis, and the expression would require taking the cube root of a complex number.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Parent |first1=James T. |title=Exact values for the sin of all integers |url=https://www.intmath.com/blog/wp-content/images/2011/06/exact-values-sin-degrees.pdf |website=Interactive Mathematics |access-date=5 February 2024 |date=June 2011}}</ref><ref name="Kowalski">{{cite journal |last1=Kowalski |first1=Travis |title=The Sine of a Single Degree |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |date=November 2016 |volume=47 |issue=5 |pages=322–332 |doi=10.4169/college.math.j.47.5.322 |s2cid=125810699 |url=https://maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/awards/college.math.j.47.5.322.pdf}}</ref>

Alternatively, by [[De Moivre's formula]]:

:<math>\begin{align}
(\cos(1^\circ) + i \sin(1^\circ))^3 &= \cos(3^\circ) + i \sin(3^\circ), \\[4mu]
(\cos(1^\circ) - i \sin(1^\circ))^3 &= \cos(3^\circ) - i \sin(3^\circ).
\end{align}</math>

Taking cube roots and adding or subtracting the equations, we have:<ref name="Kowalski"/>

:<math>\begin{align}
\cos(1^\circ) &= \;\frac{1}{2} \left(
     \sqrt[3]{\cos(3^\circ) + i \sin(3^\circ)}
   + \sqrt[3]{\cos(3^\circ) - i \sin(3^\circ)} \right),
\\[5mu]
\sin(1^\circ) &= \frac{1}{2i}\left(
     \sqrt[3]{\cos(3^\circ) + i \sin(3^\circ)}
   - \sqrt[3]{\cos(3^\circ) - i \sin(3^\circ)} \right).
\end{align}</math>
